name: Onion juice for hair

lead: Onion juice for hair is a home remedy where juice pressed from raw onion is applied to the scalp. People use it hoping to improve thinning hair or patchy loss, which is where the appearance goal lies: fuller-looking hair and a denser hairline.

The idea is long-standing in folk practice. One clinical trial published in 2002 compared crude onion juice with tap water in people with patchy alopecia areata; evidence for ordinary pattern hair loss is not established in that literature.

paras: Practitioners grate or blend onions, strain the juice, and massage it into the scalp for a period before washing it out, often several times a week for weeks or months. Some mix it with oils, honey or aloe, and many comment on the smell that lingers on hair.

Raw onion can irritate the scalp or cause contact dermatitis in some people, and the odor is a common complaint. Hair loss with a medical cause is evaluated by dermatologists, who also treat established options.

angle.text: People apply it to the scalp in the hope of regrowth or thicker hair. The only clinical trial identified studied patchy alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition, rather than male pattern baldness.

lead: Onion juice for hair is a folk treatment in which crude juice from raw onion (Allium cepa) is applied to the scalp. People use it to try to slow thinning, encourage regrowth in bald patches and make hair look thicker, so it falls within hair-loss self-care.

Interest in it among hair-loss communities grows from one clinical study. In 2002, Sharquie and Al-Obaidi published a trial in the Journal of Dermatology testing topical crude onion juice against tap water in patchy alopecia areata.[1] No trial has established the practice for common androgenetic hair loss.
infobox: Food ingredient; not an approved hair-loss drug

paras: The preparation is simple: fresh onion is grated or blended, the pulp is strained, and the liquid is applied to the scalp and left on for some time before shampooing. Users often describe repeating this regularly and commonly note the strong smell, which they try to mask with oils or rinses.

Proponents attribute effects to the sulfur-containing compounds in onion and to scalp-stimulating or antimicrobial action. Such mechanisms are proposed in popular discussion rather than demonstrated in published human work.
Fresh onion preparations can irritate skin, and sensitive people can develop contact reactions on the scalp. The odor is the most common practical objection.

A 2002 clinical trial by Sharquie and Al-Obaidi in the Journal of Dermatology tested topical crude onion juice against tap water in patchy alopecia areata, in two groups of patients.[1] No trial of onion juice for androgenetic alopecia was found.

timeline.event: Sharquie and Al-Obaidi publish a trial of topical crude onion juice for alopecia areata in the Journal of Dermatology.[1]
